answers.question: Actual pricing of Mutflex/SaudiSoftware.co/Daftra's maintenance module — not confirmed, needed to know if a cheaper entrant is even possible
answers.answer: Could not get a maintenance-module-specific price for any of the three. What was found: (1) Daftra's general ERP plans (which include the maintenance/support-center module as one of many verticals, not a separate SKU) were reported in aggregator search snippets as Advanced Plan ≈270 SAR/month and Unlimited Plan ≈350 SAR/month, with a top 'Business' tier requiring a sales quote — this came from a search-engine summary of 3rd-party listings (TrustRadius/Zoftware/Capterra), not a direct fetch of daftra.com/plans (the live page could not be fetched — proxy blocked it), so treat as WEAK/unconfirmed. (2) Mutflex has a public pricing page (mutflex.com/pricing) and offers a free 2-month trial and claims 'no hidden fees,' but no exact SAR figures appeared in any search snippet or could be fetched (page blocked). (3) SaudiSoftware.co does not publish maintenance-module pricing at all — it is a custom-development shop that quotes per-project after a contact form (one search snippet even cited a generic app-dev quote of ~15,000 SAR for a basic maintenance app with client+technician app+admin panel, which is a one-time custom-build cost, not a SaaS price). Net: there is no confirmed cheap public SaaS price point to undercut with certainty; Daftra's ~270-350 SAR/month (if accurate) sets a plausible ceiling that a lean solo-founder tool (aiming e.g. <100 SAR/month) could undercut, but this specific number is unverified from a primary source.

answers.question: Whether Daftra's maintenance-center module is oriented toward walk-in repair shops (e.g., device repair) rather than field technicians visiting customer sites — this distinction could preserve or close the wedge
answers.answer: Daftra's maintenance offering is explicitly built around a physical 'center' (مركز الصيانة / 'maintenance and support centers') and around auto-repair workshops — i.e., a walk-in model, not a mobile field-service model. Its own feature copy talks about: maintaining a list of vehicle/device owners and their history, setting maintenance appointments 'by date and time' at the shop, managing an on-site spare-parts/inventory, assigning staff/technicians within the center with role-based permissions, invoicing at the center, and notifying customers of repair status — all framed around a customer bringing the item to a location, not around a technician traveling to the customer's site with GPS tracking or live 'en route / arrived / job started' status. By contrast, a genuinely field-service-oriented Saudi app found in search (Maaloom) explicitly advertises real-time technician location states ('في الطريق، يبدأ العمل، أنهى المهمة بنجاح') and digital signed visit reports — features absent from Daftra's maintenance/auto-maintenance product pages. This supports that Daftra's module targets walk-in repair centers (auto workshops, device/support centers) rather than dispatch-and-route field technician operations, which keeps the field-technician-scheduling/dispatch wedge more open than if Daftra already covered it.

answers.question: True price sensitivity and switching willingness of 1-10 technician operators
answers.answer: No direct pricing/willingness-to-pay figures were found for micro maintenance operators (1-10 technicians) in Saudi Arabia. Indirect signal from Mostaql (freelance marketplace) project listings: small maintenance/operations companies post one-off requests for very basic tools — e.g. a company wanting to replace paper-based technician follow-up with a simple electronic system ('برنامج لمتابعة الصيانة الشهرية' for a lift/elevator maintenance business) and another explicitly asking for an Excel-sheet-based tracker ('برنامج أو شيت إكسيل لمتابعة الصيانة الشهرية') rather than a subscription SaaS product. This suggests at least some small operators prefer a low one-time freelance/Excel cost over a recurring SaaS fee, i.e., meaningful price sensitivity and reluctance to commit to monthly subscriptions — but the actual project budgets on these Mostaql listings could not be retrieved (fetch budget exhausted), so the magnitude of sensitivity and actual switching willingness from tools like Daftra/Mutflex is not confirmed. This is WEAK/indirect evidence of a problem (price-sensitive segment exists) but does NOT prove anyone will pay a recurring fee for a new tool.

Fetch budget (6/6) was exhausted before Mostaql project pages could be opened to confirm actual client-stated budgets for maintenance-tracking freelance requests, so price-sensitivity evidence remains indirect/unconfirmed.
No SAR pricing at all was found for Mutflex's maintenance/technician-tracking tiers or for SaudiSoftware.co's maintenance module (custom-quote only, no public price list).
No direct survey, review, or forum post from an actual 1-10-technician Saudi operator discussing willingness to pay for or switch away from a maintenance SaaS tool was found.
